reading.body:
AI litigation is being organized into two layers: live dockets across eleven claim families, and a small set of older precedents that decide them.

The claim families span copyright, right of publicity, product liability and wrongful death, hiring discrimination, biometric privacy, securities fraud, trade secrets, platform access, patent, consumer protection, and government contracts. That range matters because it shows AI disputes are not one legal question. They are many separate causes of action, each with its own doctrine and its own exposure.

The defenses rest on decisions made long before generative models existed. Sony supplies substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books supply transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ cover scraping, and Zeran covers Section 230. Each profile states what the case held, why AI defendants cite it, and where the analogy is weakest. The weakness is the useful part, because a precedent stretched too far is where a defense fails.

What this does not cover is outcomes. The data describes how cases are labeled and which precedents are invoked, not who won, what was awarded, or how any of it affects the cost of compute, buildings, or power. The litigation layer sits downstream of the physical buildout, and nothing here measures that link.
